examples.problem_statement: A sum of Rs 39 was divided among 45 boys and girls. Each girl gets 50 P, whereas each boy gets one rupee. How many girls are there?

solution.description: Convert the total Rs 39 into 3900 paise and divide by the 45 heads to get the average number of paise received per person.
Write the two ingredient values in the same unit as the mean: a boy's share is 100 paise and a girl's share is 50 paise.
Take the two cross differences of the alligation: mean minus the girl's value gives the boys' share of the ratio, and the boy's value minus the mean gives the girls' share.
Clear the common denominator 3 and reduce the cross differences to the simplest whole-number ratio of boys to girls.
Split the 45 children in the ratio 11 : 4 by multiplying the total by the girls' part over the 15 total parts.

key_reminders: Bring both ingredient values and the mean to one unit (paise) before applying alligation.
The cross differences give the ratio of the quantities, with each difference belonging to the opposite ingredient.
The mean here is a per-head value, so the ratio parts sum to the number of people, not to the money.
common_mistakes: Leaving Rs 39 unconverted and mixing rupees with the 50 P and 100 P values.
Reading the ratio 11 : 4 as girls : boys and answering 33 instead of 12.
Rounding the non-integer mean \frac{260}{3} to 87 paise, which breaks the exact cross differences.

concept.technique_name: triangle area with alternate base-height pairs

examples.problem_statement: Quantity A: The product of BE and AC. Quantity B: The product of BC and AD. (A) Quantity A is greater. (B) Quantity B is greater. (C) The two quantities are equal. (D) The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.

solution.result: BE is a height, AC is the base it falls on
solution.description: Look at Quantity A and identify each segment in the figure: BE is the height of the triangle and AC is the corresponding base.
Put that base and height into the triangle area formula and move the 2 across, so Quantity A is exactly twice the area.
Now treat BC as the base; AD is the height drawn to that base, so the same area formula makes Quantity B twice the area as well.
Compare the two results: both products equal twice the area of the same triangle, so neither quantity can be larger.

key_reminders: Area of a triangle is \frac{1}{2} \times \text{base} \times \text{height}, so base times height is always twice the area.
Any side of a triangle can serve as the base, paired with the height drawn to that side.
A quantitative comparison can be settled by identity alone, with no numeric values needed.
common_mistakes: Pairing BE with BC or AD with AC, mixing a height with a base it is not perpendicular to.
Choosing (D) because no side lengths are given, even though both products reduce to the same area expression.

examples.problem_statement: For how many integers n, will the inequality (n - 5)(n - 10) - 3(n - 2) \le 0 be satisfied?

solution.description: Expand the product of the two brackets and distribute the -3 across the second bracket, keeping the inequality sign unchanged.
Collect the like terms: the n terms combine to -18n and the constants combine to +56.
Split the middle term into -14n and -4n so the quadratic factorises into two linear brackets.
The product of the two brackets is negative or zero only between the roots, so n lies in the closed interval from 4 to 14.
Count the integers in that closed interval, including both endpoints, to get the number of values of n.

key_reminders: An upward-opening quadratic is \le 0 exactly on the closed interval between its roots.
Both endpoints are included because the inequality is \le, not <.
The count of integers from a to b inclusive is b - a + 1.
common_mistakes: Forgetting to distribute the -3 over both terms of (n - 2) and getting n^2 - 18n + 44.
Answering 10 by omitting one endpoint when counting the integers from 4 to 14.
Taking the solution set outside the roots instead of between them.
